summary:
TARS Care – AI Astronaut Health Companion is an intelligent health monitoring and self-assessment application designed to support astronauts during space missions. It provides a unified platform for recording health measurements, monitoring physiological and psychological wellbeing, and identifying potential health concerns.

TARS Care monitors key indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, body temperature, sleep, mood and stress. It uses rule-based assessment, personal health baselines and trend analysis to identify unusual changes and potential risks. By incorporating research from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency, TARS Care connects health changes to spaceflight hazards such as microgravity, isolation and confinement. Its AI assistant retrieves relevant medical knowledge, explains assessment results and provides evidence-informed health guidance.

Designed with offline capabilities, TARS Care supports health monitoring even when communication with Earth is limited. It is important because astronauts operate in challenging environments where immediate medical assistance may not always be available. TARS Care aims to improve health awareness, support informed self-assessment and facilitate timely medical escalation during space missions.
details:
1. What does TARS Care do and how does it work?

TARS Care is an offline-first, AI-assisted astronaut health-monitoring and self-assessment web application designed to support crew members during long-duration deep-space missions, including future Mars expeditions. It addresses the challenges of delayed communication and limited access to immediate medical support by providing an onboard platform for health monitoring, self-assessment, personal wellbeing and evidence-informed guidance.

The system monitors physiological and psychological indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep duration, mood, stress and reported symptoms. It also incorporates relevant environmental and space-weather information to provide additional mission context.

Astronauts can record health information through three workflows: simulated or connected medical devices, guided examination workflows such as the SANS Amsler grid and ocular/ultrasound assessment interfaces, and manual entry or CSV/JSON data import.

TARS Care evaluates incoming measurements using a deterministic, rule-based assessment engine. It compares readings against calibrated individual baselines, considers the current gravity environment (0g, 0.38g or 1g), and reviews 7-, 14- and 30-Sol trends. Instead of assessing each indicator independently, it identifies combined changes across physiological, psychological and environmental data, relating them to NASA's five human-spaceflight hazards.

The system also provides prototype EVA readiness classifications (GO, CAUTION and HOLD) and estimates predictive threshold runways for selected indicators, such as cabin CO₂ and sleep debt. Radiation-related assessments use available radiation measurements and space-weather context rather than treating solar events as direct measurements of crew exposure.

Its offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant retrieves relevant information from a locally available NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) research corpus. It explains assessment findings with document citations ([DOC-ID]) and provides appropriate next-step and medical-escalation guidance.

In addition to physical health monitoring, TARS Care offers a Personal Companionship and Wellbeing feature. Astronauts can write private journal entries, complete daily mood check-ins, respond to guided reflection prompts and interact with a conversational AI companion. The system visualises self-reported mood and wellbeing trends to help astronauts recognise changes throughout their missions.

2. What benefits does it have?

TARS Care offers several benefits:

  • Continuous health awareness: Provides a centralised overview of physiological and psychological wellbeing.
  • Early identification of potential concerns: Highlights unusual measurements and changes from individual baselines.
  • Personalised assessment: Considers individual health history, gravity environment and longitudinal trends.
  • Evidence-informed guidance: Uses NASA and CSA research to explain findings and support recommendations.
  • Medical autonomy: Supports initial onboard self-assessment when immediate communication with Earth is unavailable.
  • Emotional companionship: Provides journaling, mood check-ins, guided reflection and conversational AI support.
  • Wellbeing tracking: Visualises self-reported mood and emotional wellbeing trends over time.
  • Crew and privacy support: Provides multi-crew triage for Crew Medical Officers (CMOs), onboard med-kit reserve tracking and access-controlled private behavioural journals.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact of TARS Care is to strengthen astronaut health awareness, support informed self-assessment, and facilitate timely medical escalation during long-duration deep-space missions.

NASA identifies five major hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. These hazards can affect cardiovascular function, neuro-ocular health, bone and muscle health, sleep, and psychological wellbeing.

By combining multi-indicator health monitoring, personal baseline tracking, offline medical knowledge retrieval and emotional wellbeing support, TARS Care helps astronauts recognise potential health changes and understand when further attention may be needed.

Its personal companionship feature also addresses the psychological challenges of prolonged isolation and confinement by providing a private space for self-expression, reflection and emotional support.

Beyond space exploration, TARS Care demonstrates how offline-resilient and personalised health decision-support systems could benefit people working in remote or resource-limited environments on Earth.

4. What tools, programming languages and technologies were used?

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Host Grotesk and Recharts for dashboards, health trends and interactive body-map exploration.

Backend: Python, FastAPI and Pydantic for REST APIs, health assessment, EVA readiness logic and data validation.

Local persistence: SQLite (tarscare_local.db) for crew profiles, synthetic telemetry, baselines, examinations, inventory and synchronisation queues.

Assessment engine: Python-based deterministic rules, personal baseline comparison, multi-indicator correlation and trend analysis.

Offline RAG: TF-IDF lexical retrieval and locally cached all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings for NASA and CSA document retrieval.

Local AI: Optional Ollama inference (/api/chat) with a deterministic fallback and citation/safety checks.

Space data integration: NASA DONKI space-weather feeds and NASA InSight historical Mars environmental data, with local caching.

Personal wellbeing: Private journaling, mood check-ins, guided reflection prompts, conversational AI and mood-trend visualisation.

Voice and accessibility: Web Speech API readout and voice symptom capture, alongside high-contrast EVA emergency mode.

The demonstration database contains 30 Sols of synthetic Mars mission telemetry (Sol 155–184), together with crew profiles, calibrated baselines and other operational records.

The system is designed for local data storage and essential offline assessment. NASA API information is cached locally when available, while local RAG retrieval and assessment functionality reduce reliance on continuous internet connectivity.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

TARS Care goes beyond conventional fitness or clinical dashboards by combining multi-indicator health assessment, spaceflight hazard context, offline AI knowledge retrieval and personal companionship in one astronaut-centred application.

  • Three-question crew wayfinding and interactive body map: Organises the Mission Overview around three questions: How am I doing? What has changed? Should I take action? An interactive seven-region body map helps astronauts explore potential health concerns.
  • Cross-indicator and hazard synthesis: Connects physiological, behavioural and environmental signals, such as increased heart rate alongside reduced sleep and elevated stress.
  • Offline-first AI with safety controls: Combines local hybrid retrieval and optional local LLM explanations with deterministic fallback, source citations and non-diagnostic safety boundaries.
  • Personal AI companionship: Offers private journaling, daily mood tracking, guided reflection and conversational AI support to address psychological wellbeing during isolation and confinement.
  • Wellbeing trend analysis: Transforms daily self-reported mood and wellbeing entries into visual trends, helping astronauts recognise patterns over time.
  • Space-data integration: Incorporates NASA DONKI space-weather information and historical Mars environmental observations to provide additional mission context.
  • Device catalogue and store-and-forward operations: Separates simulated demonstration data from user-entered and device-imported readings, and simulates communication delays and blackouts through queued medical consultation packets.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Medical safety and non-diagnostic boundaries: TARS Care is a prototype decision-support tool, not clinically certified flight software. It uses an IMMEDIATE > HIGH > ROUTINE priority hierarchy, suppresses routine exercise recommendations during critical warning conditions and avoids medication dosing or surgical instructions.
  • Scientific and unit integrity: Separates absorbed radiation dose (Gy / mGy) from equivalent or effective dose (Sv / mSv). It avoids presenting prototype thresholds as official NASA medical limits and distinguishes real research from synthetic demonstration data.
  • Data provenance and transparency: Labels information as Simulated Data, User-Entered Data, Real Research Data or System Operational Spec, preventing synthetic records from being mistaken for actual astronaut measurements.
  • Psychological wellbeing and privacy: Provides access-controlled personal journals and mood records, with clear separation between private content and information available to CMO triage or Earth-sync consultation packets.
  • AI reliability: Keeps the rule-based safety engine responsible for assessment severity. The AI assistant explains findings but cannot override safety classifications or issue unsupported medical instructions.
  • Human factors and accessibility: Uses a dark-mode interface (#0B0D1A / #121522), tabular numerals, clear health-status indicators and high-contrast emergency mode to support usability in spacecraft environments.
  • Offline resilience: Prioritises local data storage, cached scientific references, local assessment and queued synchronisation to maintain essential functions during communication interruptions.
